editing.text: In my opinion, I think a part-time job teaches students something that no classroom can. My neighbour Dũng, who is nineteen, works three evenings a week in a small bookshop near the university. He says the job has changed him, and he is now very interesting in publishing as a career. His manager told me that Dũng is a very success employee, mainly because he never arrives late. He handles complaints very calm, even when the shop is crowded on Saturday afternoons. Of course, a heavy work schedule can have a bad affect on marks. Last term Dũng lost the last bus home twice and reached his room after midnight, so he slept through a whole morning of lectures. Its true that some employers in the area pay badly and change the hours at the last minute. Their are clear rules about how many hours a student may work, but almost nobody reads them. We discussed about this problem in our citizenship lesson on Tuesday, and the whole class had an opinion. Our teacher said that a student who is good in maths can find tutoring work very easily, and that tutoring is more easier to fit around a timetable than shift work. She asked us to send our short reports in Friday evening so that she could read them at the weekend. She also mentioned that the college plans to rise the number of paid internships next year. For students who live in the outer districts, buses are an economic way to reach the industrial park, although the journey is slow. Whether Dũng keeps his job next term depends of the exam timetable, but he says he would miss the shop if he left.

errors.reason: *In my opinion* and *I think* say the same thing; keep one of them.
*-ed* describes how a person feels; *-ing* describes the thing that causes the feeling.
A word in front of a noun has to be the adjective form, *successful*.
The word describes how he handles complaints, so it takes the adverb form.
*effect* is the noun (*an effect on*); *affect* is the verb.
You *miss* a bus, a class or a chance; you *lose* an object you owned.
*It's* is short for *it is*; *its* with no apostrophe means "belonging to it".
*There* introduces existence; *their* is the possessive of *they*.
*discuss* takes a direct object with no preposition.
*good* is followed by *at* for a skill or a subject.
Short adjectives take -er on their own; *more* as well as -er marks the comparison twice.
*on* goes with a named day or date, even when a part of the day follows it.
*raise* takes an object (*raise the number*); *rise* never does.

items.sentence: The documentary about coral reefs in Nha Trang was very interested.
items.reason: The documentary causes the feeling, so it takes the -ing form.

items.sentence: Nga gave a confident presentation and answered every question clear.
items.reason: The word describes how she answered, so it needs the adverb form.

items.stem: The committee praised the ___ of the new recycling scheme.
items.reason: After *the* and before *of*, the slot needs a noun.

items.stem: Traffic in the city centre is ___ than it was five years ago.
items.reason: *bad* has the irregular comparative *worse*, and it never takes *more* as well.

items.stem: ___ public transport should be cheaper for students under eighteen.
items.reason: One marker of opinion is enough; doubling it weakens the sentence.

items.sentence: Their are several reasons why young people move to the big cities.
The new policy will effect every secondary school in the province.
items.reason: *affect* is the verb; *effect* is normally the noun.

items.stem: Solar panels are an ___ choice for families who want a smaller electricity bill.
items.reason: *economical* means "it saves money"; *economic* relates to the economy.

items.stem: The company plans to ___ wages by five per cent in April.
items.reason: *raise* takes an object, and *wages* is the object here.

items.sentence: I lost the train to Vinh because the taxi got stuck in the morning traffic.
items.reason: You *miss* a train you failed to catch; you *lose* something you owned.

items.sentence: Please arrive to the hall ten minutes before the ceremony starts.
items.reason: *arrive* takes *at* for a building or a point, and *in* for a town or a country.

items.sentence: We discussed about the proposal for almost an hour without agreeing.
items.reason: *discuss* is followed straight by its object, with no preposition.

items.stem: The success of the project depends ___ how many volunteers sign up.
items.reason: *depend* always takes *on*; learn the verb and its preposition together.

items.stem: The results will be published ___ the morning of 12 May.
items.reason: A part of the day normally takes *in*, but a part of a named date takes *on*.

items.stem: My cousin has been interested ___ marine biology since she was twelve.
